7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers blueprint around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Recent findings suggest that actual development rarely follows that proposal. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

According to recent reports, historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

In a recent development, completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

In a recent development, actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

In a recent development, carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production challenges. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing latest features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

Sources indicate that these records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual problem could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

In a recent development, historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating new tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

Industry observers note that for example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the fresh estimate.

Recent findings suggest that however, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The new integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying issue.

In a recent development, research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

According to recent reports, for example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

According to recent reports, the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

For example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

According to recent reports, suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

In such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that however, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Recent findings suggest that teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as important inputs to sprint forecasting.

It has been revealed that when you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

Industry observers note that historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

It has been revealed that however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

Sources indicate that with this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

Recent findings suggest that however, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

According to recent reports, apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a initiative, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

According to recent reports, ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

It has been revealed that not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Recent findings suggest that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

According to recent reports, 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning highlights whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

It has been revealed that 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

These metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

Industry observers note that **3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

According to recent reports, teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

Recent findings suggest that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

Industry observers note that 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data indicates how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings.
  • Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics.
  • Industry observers note that A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone.

Industry observers note that A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Recent findings suggest that traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

It has been revealed that "The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," claims Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information.

Sources indicate that to make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

It has been revealed that "Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster.

It has been revealed that working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

Sources indicate that chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," notes Lei Du.

Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut.

The fresh approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

Industry observers note that these gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

Sources indicate that "You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," states Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers.

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

Industry observers note that "A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an key role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control.

*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

Recent findings suggest that one method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

In a recent development, the scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

American Airlines has responded after passengers found that their bags had been covered in a brown, liquid-like substance while waiting two hours for them.

Industry observers note that when you get off a flight, there can be a sense of trepidation about what’s to come next. If you land at the wrong time, you’ll be stuck in a long security queue, meaning your bags might end up stuck on the reclaim belt or even taken somewhere else.

Well, for passengers on an American Airlines flight from Miami to Atlanta, they ended up having a two-hour wait for their bags after landing. Yet, that wasn’t the biggest issue.

Sources indicate that as TikToker Derick McCallum, who had been aboard the plane, noted, the bags ended up coming out looking like they’d been covered in poop. “Underneath the flight, it flooded. The doo-doo water got all in the bottom,” McCallum stated. “Now they’re bringing the bags out; there is doo-doo on the bags.”.

The TikToker’s video has racked up more than 1.3 million views, as of writing, with plenty of viewers commenting with their dismay at the claims.

However, an American Airlines spokesperson confirmed that it wasn’t feces on the bags, but rather liquefied peanut butter.

“Unfortunately, a food item from a customer’s checked bag leaked during the flight, affecting several bags nearby,” a spokesperson told the Newly introduced York Post. “Our team will work directly with the affected customers to make it right.”.

Accelerate ND-Parallel: A guide to Efficient Multi-GPU Training

📅 08 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies.
  • We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.
  • To further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies. In Accelerate, together with Axolotl, we have integrated a quick and easy way to use any combination of parallelism strategies in your training script!

Here is how to add it to your training script:.

We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.

To further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl. To help you get started right away we've tested some example configs which you can modify to suit your needs - try one out with:.

You can also check out the Axolotl ND-Parallelism docs for more details - adding ND parallel techniques to your existing configs is as simple as adding one or more of the following fields to your Axolotl config file:.

Industry observers note that we've made it easy to configure the degrees of different parallelism strategies and how they are combined through the ParallelismConfig class in Accelerate, or through config fields in Axolotl, but how do we know which configuration will work best for our use case? As we scale to training models with tens or even hundreds of billions of parameters, the primary challenge comes from understanding the different parallelism strategies and how they interact to minimise communication overhead across devices. In this post, we'll walk through how the different parallelism strategies work, and when and how you might want to compose them.

In a recent development, data parallelism (DP) is the most common technique for training models across multiple GPUs, and involves replicating the model, gradients and optimizer states across each device, whilst evenly distributing data batches between GPUs, and synchronising gradients across devices before updating parameters. This can significantly increase throughput compared to single-device training, but requires that your model is able to fit on a single device.

We can control the number of replicas of the model with the dp_replicate_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or config field in Axolotl. It's worth noting that DP is a top-most-level parallelism strategy, meaning that if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and we compose it with other parallelism strategies, there would be 2 replicas of the model, each also influenced by the other parallelism strategies. For example, if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and tp_size=2, we would have 2 replicas of the model, each with 2 tensor parallel shards.

We use the term shard to describe data on a single device which is a partition of a larger piece of data.

Sources indicate that what if our model is too large to fit on a single device? Fully sharded data parallel (FSDP) addresses this issue by sharding (distributing evenly) the model’s weights, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs (this is inspired by DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-3), whilst each device still receives its portion of the full batch of data. As you may notice from the diagram above, rather than requiring a full copy of the entire model on each device, we only gather the weights for a single layer at a time before the forward pass, after which the weights may be sharded again.

In this way, we trade memory usage for the communication overhead of gathering sharded parameters before each forward and backward pass, and reduce-scatter-ing local gradients. We can control this trade-off in FSDP by tuning the granularity at which parameters are gathered. On one extreme, we can gather and re-shard every layer of our model, which would result in the lowest peak memory usage, but incur the highest communication costs. In practice, a common approach is to gather the weights for an entire transformer decoder block at a time.

Whilst we can make further memory-compute trade-offs and offload model parameters and gradients to the CPU to train larger models, this can be prohibitively slow. Instead, let’s consider how we can effectively utilise even more devices to train larger models whilst maintaining high data throughput.

It has been revealed that we use the term node to refer to a single machine which hosts multiple GPUs (up to a maximum of 8), with fast intra-node communication channels using e.g. NVLink between GPUs. When using multiple nodes for training, we rely on relatively slower inter-node communication channels between machines using e.g. Infiniband. We also refer to the total number of devices in the process pool as the world size - e.g. a single node with 8 GPUs represents a world size of 8, and 4 nodes would represent a world size of 32.

When using FSDP across multiple nodes, we treat the entire set of devices across nodes as if we were training on a single node. For example, with 4 nodes containing 8 GPUs each, we perform our sharding across 32 devices, and perform our collective all-reduce and reduce-scatter operations using both inter-and-intra-node communication backends. In this manner, FSDP alone can scale to a substantial number of GPUs with a large global batch size to increase data throughput. However, there comes a point where several challenges arise that may require composing FSDP with other parallelism techniques. We usually try to avoid doing FSDP across more than a full node, as the communication overhead can become too high, we'll talk about how to address this in the section on Hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism.

You can use the dp_shard_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig together with a prepared FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin, or set the dp_shard_size config field in Axolotl to set the degree of FSDP applied to your model.

Tensor Parallel (TP) is a kind of model parallelism technique, where shards of the model permanently live on separate devices, and in contrast to data parallel techniques, each device receives an identical batch of data. TP works by distributing the computation of linear layers across devices, so each device only computes a portion of the matrix multiplication. This technique works best when there are large linear layers, such as the feed-forward layers in transformer models, which can be split across devices. We can also use TP on each of the query, key, value, and output projections in the attention layers with almost no extra communication cost.

To achieve the best performance, parameters of consecutive layers can be distributed in a specific fashion, minimizing the required communication. When working with pairs of linear layers, we can split the first layer column-wise, and the subsequent layer row-wise, allowing us to compute the output with only a single all-reduce operation to combine the sharded outputs.

In a recent development, unlike the dynamic sharding behaviour of FSDP, TP creates static memory partitions which result in a constant memory usage reduction scaling with the TP group size. This becomes crucial for massive models where even a single decoder layer is too large to fit into memory during the FSDP all-gather (recall that common practice in FSDP is to gather the weights of an entire decoder layer at a time). However, unlike FSDP which scales relatively linearly across nodes (up to a point - ~512 GPUs on a homogenous cluster, significantly less across lower-bandwidth connections), TP is only effective within the boundaries of a single node. TP requires frequent activation synchronization between devices during computation, as each device computes only a portion of the output, requiring the outputs from other devices to be communicated before continuing the forward pass. Thus, if we wish to utilise TP in a multi-node setup, we must consider composing TP with other parallelism techniques, while keeping TP only within a single node. Due to its large communications overhead, TP is not recommended for PCIe linked GPUs.

In Accelerate, the TP size is configured through tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the tensor_parallel_size config field.

Recently, reasoning capabilities in LLMs resulted in sequence lengths skyrocketing as models use more and more tokens to solve complex tasks. To achieve this behaviour through fine-tuning, we need a way to train models on very large sequence lengths - which can sometimes reach up to a million tokens!

Since the attention operation in transformers scales quadratically with context length, this becomes impossible on a single GPU. For example, when fine-tuning a relatively small model such as Mistral-7B (which uses 32 attention heads), if we use a sequence length of 128k a single attention matrix will utilise 128k * 128k * 2 bytes * num_heads=32 = ~32GB * 32 = ~1TB of activations memory! Whilst this example is not realistic when using optimised attention implementations such as FlashAttention, it helps illustrate the growth in memory requirements from increasing the context length.

With context parallelism (CP), we can shard the inputs across the sequence dimension, resulting in each device only processing a chunk of the full context and computing a smaller portion of the full, prohibitively large, attention matrix. To see how this works, recall that the attention computation is described by the equation: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}(QK^T)V Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V.

Where Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V are the query, key, and value matrices respectively. Each query vector (row, or input embedding) of Q Q Q must compute the attention scores against every key vector of K K K in the entire sequence to correctly apply the softmax normalisation. These attention scores are then weighted with all value vectors in V V V.

The crucial detail here lies in the fact that each row in Q Q Q can compute its attention score independently of one another, but each query vector still requires the full K K K and V V V matrices. In other words, given an input with sequence length $n$, we can expand our above attention equation as:.

Attention(Q,K,V)1=softmax(Q1KT)VAttention(Q,K,V)2=softmax(Q2KT)V⋮Attention(Q,K,V)n=softmax(QnKT)V \begin{align} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_1 &= \text{softmax}(Q_1 K^T) V \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_2 &= \text{softmax}(Q_2 K^T) V \\ &\vdots \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_n &= \text{softmax}(Q_n K^T) V \end{align} Attention(Q,K,V)1​Attention(Q,K,V)2​Attention(Q,K,V)n​​=softmax(Q1​KT)V=softmax(Q2​KT)V⋮=softmax(Qn​KT)V​​.

Sources indicate that where we denote each row of the query matrix as Q1,Q2,...,Qn Q_1, Q_2, ..., Q_n Q1​,Q2​,...,Qn​. This can be generalized as: Attention(Q,K,V)i=softmax(QiKT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_i = \text{softmax}(Q_i K^T) V \quad \forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., n\} Attention(Q,K,V)i​=softmax(Qi​KT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n}.

Recent findings suggest that when we shard the inputs across devices, the resulting Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V matrices (computed from these input shards) are also automatically sharded along the sequence dimension - each GPU computes queries, keys, and values only for its portion of the sequence. For example, with a world size of W W W GPUs and sequence length n n n:.

In a recent development, how do we ensure the attention is computed correctly? As established above, each device only needs its own shard of Q Q Q, but requires the full K K K and V V V matrices to compute the attention correctly. We can achieve this by using a technique called RingAttention, which works as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that accelerate enables this with the accelerator.maybe_context_parallel decorator, which is also showcased in the Accelerate example script. You can also learn more about how it works and its limitations in our CP concept guide.

Similar to TP, in Accelerate the CP size is configured through cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the context_parallel_size config field.

In the multi-node setting, data parallel techniques such as FSDP treat the entire network topology as if it existed along a single dimension. You may find this approach limiting for a variety of reasons:.

To try and address some of these problems, we can think of multi-node clusters as having a two-dimensional topology: fast intra-node communication between devices along one axis, and relatively slower inter-node communication along another axis. Let’s consider how we can compose the parallelism techniques we’ve introduced so far to take advantage of this.

Hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism (HSDP) is a kind of 2D parallelism which performs FSDP within a node, and DP across nodes - that is to say the model is replicated across each node, and sharded using FSDP within each node. This allows the greater communication overhead of FSDP to utilize the faster intra-node links, whilst DP minimises the slower inter-node communication overhead to a single gradient synchronisation step. You might consider this approach if you were facing problem 1 and wished to speed up training at the cost of increased memory usage.

Sources indicate that it’s notable to note that we can freely configure the shape of our 2D network topology, as we aren’t constrained to the dimensions being aligned with physical node boundaries - you might apply FSDP across 2 nodes whilst replicating across groups of 2 nodes, which would result in lower memory usage but slower throughput, but still reduce the intra-node FSDP communication overhead by a factor of two. This is a knob we encourage you to tune to your specific hardware setup and fine-tuning needs.

You can enable HSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and dp_replicate_size in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or through Axolotl's config fields.

Industry observers note that as we mentioned earlier, TP should be applied within a node to utilize the high-bandwidth intra-node communications, thus, combining TP and FSDP involves sharding the model across nodes using FSDP, and within a node using TP. To a certain degree, this potentially offers a neat solution to all three of the concerns above: the latency costs from FSDP could be reduced by a factor of 8, layers that are too large to fit on a single device are now evenly distributed across devices, and since each TP group receives an identical batch of data, we can also reduce our global batch size by a factor of 8. However, if this remains insufficient, we are unable to increase the TP size across nodes and must consider an alternative approach.

In Accelerate you can combine TP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

This is a 2D parallelism strategy that combines FSDP and CP, and while this is not very commonly used as CP already combines with FSDP (more on why in the accelerate concept guide), it can be useful in some cases i.e. when requiring a large sequence length, consequently requiring a large cp_size. If this still doesn't fit into your memory budget, you can apply FSDP on top of this, further reducing the memory usage.

In Accelerate you can combine CP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and context_parallel_size config fields.

According to recent reports, with a sufficiently large world size (note: while the minimum world size for 3D parallelism is 8, it is most effective at much larger scales), we can consider combining HSDP with TP which creates a hierarchy where DP first replicates the model across groups of nodes, FSDP then shards the model within each group, and TP splits individual layers within each node. You might consider this approach when facing all of the scaling constraints we mentioned above, as it provides the most flexibility to adapt to your specific training setup by making trade-offs between memory usage and throughput.

In Accelerate you can combine HSDP and TP by defining all of dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tp_size in ParallelismConfig. Similarly in Axolotl you can add all of the dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

Recent findings suggest that there are additional ways to combine multiple parallelisms which we haven't covered, such as 4D parallel using HSDP + TP + CP, but they operate very similarly to the techniques we've already covered. Most of all, we encourage you to play with different techniques and configurations - this is the best way to gain an intuition for the different ways in which you can make memory/throughput trade-offs.

Below are some additional tips you may find useful when working in distributed settings:.

Industry observers note that when using FSDP and working with models that are too large to fit in a single device, enabling both CPU RAM efficient loading and sharded state dict checkpointing technique is crucial. You can enable this through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type parameters in Accelerate's FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin,.

or through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type config fields inside the fsdp_config in Axolotl:.

It has been revealed that the total batch size used during training plays an crucial factor in training stability, memory usage, and data throughput. When using DP and/or FSDP the effective batch size is calculated as:.

effective_batch_size = micro_batch_size * gradient_accumulation_steps * dp_world_size.

where dp_world_size = (dp_shard_size * dp_replicate_size) / tp_size. You can increase your batch size by increasing your total micro batch size or gradient accumulation steps in your training loop, or setting the micro_batch_size and gradient_accumulation_steps config fields in Axolotl, or increasing the total dp_world_size by adding more GPUs. As we mentioned above, this imposes a minimum total batch size of dp_world_size - when using pure DP/FSDP, this will be your total world size, and if this is too high the only way to decrease the total batch size is by introducing tensor parallelism. Finally, with a fixed number of GPUs and in memory-constrained scenarios, we recommend increasing gradient_accumulation_steps instead of micro_batch_size to achieve larger effective batch sizes, and vice-versa.

Correspondingly, when your effective batch size increases due to introducing data parallelism, you should scale your learning rate to maintain training stability. Common approaches include linear scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * (effective_batch_size / base_batch_size) or square root scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * sqrt(effective_batch_size / base_batch_size).

Sources indicate that when memory constraints persist even with parallelism strategies, gradient checkpointing can provide additional memory savings by trading compute for memory. During the forward pass, only a subset of activations are kept in memory (typically at transformer block boundaries), and intermediate activations are recomputed during the backward pass. This technique works seamlessly with all parallelism strategies covered above. In Accelerate, you can enable it by setting activation_checkpointing=true in FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin:.

Note that gradient checkpointing typically increases training time by ~20-30% due to activation recomputation, but can reduce activation memory by 60-80%, making it particularly valuable when training very large models or using long sequence lengths.

How to use accelerate config with this feature？.

Does this pipeline work for a custom model?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy.
  • According to recent reports, in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

According to recent reports, in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

Industry observers note that "The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a upcoming generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

It has been revealed that mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

Using Light Inside Computer Chips.

Sources indicate that much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

It has been revealed that the compact DTU nanolaser is an vital step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers.

Recent findings suggest that the new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

Sources indicate that at its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

Recent findings suggest that when researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use.

The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

It has been revealed that computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

#103709. Breaking: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1544 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, artificial intelligence is giving researchers a latest way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users.
  • According to recent reports, the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, artificial intelligence is giving researchers a latest way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

Recent findings suggest that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

According to recent reports, the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that shows that the method is picking up a real signal," states Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them.".

What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials.

Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify key safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

"Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns.".

The distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

"We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit customers in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating.".

Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal.

The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet people to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

It has been revealed that "Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," claims Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report.".

According to recent reports, since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more quickly when millions of people begin using a drug.

Sources indicate that "Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," states Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight.".

AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible.

One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

Patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

Researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One crucial reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and promptly.

"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," says Sehgal.

Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts.

The researchers stress that Reddit owners do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

According to recent reports, even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit customers closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

It has been revealed that about 44% of users included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.

More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

Sources indicate that nearly 4% of customers who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

Customers also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

Recent findings suggest that fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting.

Industry observers note that one possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely notable region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

According to recent reports, "These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," claims Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically.".

The researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads.

For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," says Sehgal.

The researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar says.

In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread swiftly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among customers may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move quickly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," claims Guntuku.

Industry observers note that this study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

Back in August, fans spotted what appeared to be Dexter’s apartment in GTA 6 after Rockstar released its 26-minute extended gameplay showcase.

The building closely resembled the real-life Miami apartment complex used throughout the original eight seasons of Dexter, but fans had no way of knowing whether Rockstar had included any additional references.

Now that GTA 6 has launched, players have tracked down the waterfront property and uncovered a number of Easter eggs that make the connection even clearer.

As shown in footage shared by DETONATED, players can explore the complex, which Rockstar has named “Trinity Apartments.”.

That’s a reference to the infamous Trinity Killer, Arthur Mitchell, who was played by John Lithgow in Dexter Season 4 and remains one of the show’s most iconic villains.

Dexter Easter Eggs in Grand Theft Auto 6 🔥💥 Dexter's Apartment at 'Trinity Apartments'💥 'Slice of Life' Boat💥 Tools on Roof including SyringeLocated on Washington Island (Vice Beach) pic.twitter.com/q8lnAMR3rH.

Industry observers note that although players can walk right up to Dexter’s apartment door, they can’t actually enter the property. There is an air conditioner, though, an ideal place for hiding blood slides.

Industry observers note that hidden on top of the building is what appears to be one of Dexter’s signature kill kits, containing a knife, tape, rope and a syringe. These are all tools the serial killer famously used to subdue and murder his victims throughout the series.

The references don’t end there, either. Nearby, players can find and steal a Lure Predator L35P, a boat resembling Dexter’s beloved “Slice of Life.”.

In the show, Dexter regularly used the Slice of Life to transport and dispose of his victims’ remains in the ocean. While the GTA 6 vessel doesn’t carry the same name, players can take it out onto the water and recreate some of the Bay Harbor Butcher’s infamous trips.

It’s an impressive tribute to the series, especially given that Rockstar hasn’t explicitly identified the location as Dexter’s home.

With GTA 6 only just launching, players have already begun uncovering secrets across Leonida. Fans previously spotted a Vice City Easter egg hiding in the game’s trailer, and there are likely plenty more discoveries waiting to be made.

In a recent development, you wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

Sources indicate that that is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

In a recent development, the good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

In a recent development, people often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

Sources indicate that you can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The significant mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

Microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

Recent findings suggest that send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

Recent findings suggest that SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

A basic SPF record looks like this:.

Industry observers note that DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

Your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

In a recent development, DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

Start with a monitoring policy:.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

Sources indicate that don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:.

Recent findings suggest that one more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

In a recent development, if you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

Sources indicate that A new domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

A simple schedule for a fresh domain:.

Sources indicate that send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

And if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

Sources indicate that A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

Never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

Yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

It has been revealed that most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

It has been revealed that the complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

Industry observers note that A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:.

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

Replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

Sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:.

Check them weekly, and right after any massive campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:.

It has been revealed that aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

Industry observers note that the common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a new domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

It has been revealed that DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

Yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

It has been revealed that sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

Recent findings suggest that if you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

Industry observers note that after that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.

Recent findings suggest that in AI Sheets, new columns are created by writing prompts, and you can iterate as many times as you need and edit the cells/validate cells to teach the model what you want. But more on this later!

Compare and vibe test models. Imagine you want to test the latest models on your data. You can import a dataset with prompts/questions, and create several columns (one per model) with a prompt like this: Answer the following: {{prompt}}, where prompt is a column in your dataset. You can validate the results manually or create a new column with an LLM as a judge prompt like this: Evaluate the responses to the following question: {{prompt}}. Response 1: {{model1}}. Response 2: {{model2}}, where model1 and model2 are columns in your dataset with different model responses.

Improve prompts for your data and specific models. Imagine you want to build an application to process customer requests and give automatic answers. You can load a sample dataset with customer requests and start playing and iterating with different prompts and models to generate responses. One cool feature of AI Sheets is that you can provide feedback by editing or validating cells. These example cells will be added to your prompts automatically. You can think of it as a tool to fine-tune prompts and add a few-shot examples to your prompts very efficiently, by looking at your data in real-time!

Transform a dataset. Imagine you want to clean up a column of your dataset. You can add a upcoming column with a prompt like Remove extra punctuation marks from the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to clean up.

Classify a dataset. Imagine you want to classify some content in your dataset. You can add a fresh column with a prompt like Categorize the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to categorize.

Analyze a dataset. Imagine you want to extract the main ideas in your dataset. You can add a fresh column with a prompt like this: Extract the most important ideas from the following: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to analyze.

Sources indicate that enrich a dataset. Imagine you have a dataset with addresses that are missing zip codes. You can add a new column with a prompt like this: Find the zip code of the following address: {{address}} (in this case, you must enable the "Search the web" option to ensure accurate results).

In a recent development, generate a synthetic dataset. Imagine you need a dataset with realistic emails, but the data is not available for data privacy reasons. You can create a dataset with a prompt like this: Write a short description of a professional in the field of pharma companies and name the column person_bio. Then you can create another column with a prompt like this Write a realistic professional email as it was written by the following person: {{person_bio}}.

AI Sheets gives you two ways to start: import existing data or generate a dataset from scratch. Once your data is loaded, you can refine it by adding columns, editing cells, and regenerating content.

The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange upcoming physics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics.
  • In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics.
  • The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

According to recent reports, "What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," claims lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

Recent findings suggest that when the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

"These results open a newly introduced direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics.

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

Industry observers note that more broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover fresh ways to control and study light.
