💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A latest optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles.
  • Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a upcoming type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost.
  • It has been revealed that optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A latest optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a upcoming type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring notable health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

It has been revealed that optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

Industry observers note that the researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision.

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

Recent findings suggest that to accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

In a recent development, "The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," noted Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system.".

Industry observers note that the researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

In a recent development, another crucial advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

Recent findings suggest that when used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

In a recent development, the researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

Sources indicate that "These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," remarked Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.".

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough.

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

Recent findings suggest that the Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," stated Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible.".

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices.

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

According to recent reports, healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day.".

Sources indicate that as photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a upcoming generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto 6 review

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that my best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely.
  • I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's.
  • GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that my best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a fresh 'third place': the car.

I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly big and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without.

I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5, its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't.

Reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape.

I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x'. To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.

In a recent development, whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about massive ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.

None of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything.

In a recent development, GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms.

Recent findings suggest that jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes.

What else can be said? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things.

The fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.

Buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those newly introduced wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list.

Pick up some groceries. Get those flowers. Grab some clothes for Lucia to change into. Maybe finish those odd DIY jobs you've left half-started around the place so, y'know, your bedroom actually has a wall. Ever since GTA 4, and Roman Bellic's slightly desperate calls to go play darts and shoot some pool, Rockstar has leant further and further into the mundane. But here the studio has gone many steps further, past the Sopranos of GTA 5 and poker of Red Dead Redemption 2, full-tilt into slice-of-life. The result, mercifully, is anything but dull - all these situations, familiar as they may be, are really moments for irony, humour, character, just as they are in life itself. That, and a welcome chance to catch your breath amidst the bombast, which accelerates from these early missions exponentially.

That early, to-do list mission is like a lot of other moments in GTA, in that it's a case of Rockstar not-so-subtly dropping hints. This time, it's "we are going to play with your priorities". If there's a constant in GTA 6, you realise, it's that there often seems to be a nagging thought in the back of your mind as you progress. Should I be prioritising this right now? Is that optional thing worth the effort? Will this choice matter? How? It's such a prominent thought as you play, the actual act of devising what systems this game is using as you progress is as interesting in itself as how those systems end up working. Or to put it more simply: figuring this game out for yourself is really part of the fun.

According to recent reports, back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later).

Lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff).

Sources indicate that and those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the big, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else.

Small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV demonstrates, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating.

In a recent development, none of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond.

All together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played.

According to recent reports, I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States.

Recent findings suggest that I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely latest when I drive through them again.

According to recent reports, at one point, amongst the forest of the national park up in Leonida's northern third - trundling down one winding dirt track among many, trees in all directions - I actually found myself slightly lost. At least for a moment, anyway, until I plonked down a map marker and the GPS sorted me out. GTA 6 asks more of you than any previous GTA game, but it's also a retraction from the intentional clunk of Red Dead Redemption 2. You'll never be truly stuck or stumped; there's no sense of toil.

Industry observers note that A quick example: the Scooter Bros (remember those?!) return here in a delightful reference, now acting as an official in-game phone app that lets you summon an owned vehicle for a fee, or up to three times a day if you unlock the app's "unlimited" version for a one-off cost. They can also repair your car or recover it if, like me, you have a habit of landing it on its roof. You can also fix it up at the returning Pay 'n' Spray's and all-upcoming gas stations - which, thankfully, you really don't need to visit for refuelling all that often. (When you do, it's often worth the time: this is a great window for an emergent event to pop up - more on those, too, later.).

Soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself.

Time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning prepares for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe.

Industry observers note that I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles, and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall.

This is not a patch of paint designed to be noticed. It's in the foreground for a fraction of a second as Lucia heads into another room, but it stuck for precisely that reason. This is the product of someone looking intensely at the environment as they attempt to recreate it and realising how important imperfections are to simulating reality. Clearly someone's scuffed, scratched, or graffitied something outside of this office, and the penitentiary system has felt the need to paint over it in some vain declaration of order. And then tight budgets, like a crumbling English council once again repainting a playground fence, have dictated the colour of paint that'll be used - likely whatever was to hand - to cover up these little marks of rebellion.

Sources indicate that I looked at this and wrote it down. And then a few hours later, as I was whizzing around this world evading cop cars, hopping out to make a mad dash for cover, I realised how pointless that was. I'd already been darting by piles and piles of this stuff. Back alleys filled with rubbish - glorious rubbish, the most decadent scrap metal, buckets of mulch, and sacks of rotting food waste you've ever seen - and tables covered in piles of tat. Back offices stacked with papers, posters, family photos, files, mugs, notices, trophies, pens, and all kinds of amalgamated bric-a-brac that forms a picture of a real office in the mind.

The point is: at first, as Rockstar gently guides you from place to place, gradually layering the systems onto one another, easing you into this ocean of water by toe, ankle, knee, waist, you think it's doing that thing where video games front load fidelity to set the tone, maybe flex a little, before easing up after hitting you with some big and glorious view. Then you realise this is just what this game is like. It's everywhere. A huge amount of this map is, in the nicest possible way, kind of pointless. It's things - a disused motel, a lumber mill - which have no mission or character attached, and are instead there predominantly because in a real world they would be there, and therefore, to Rockstar, they must be there.

Recent findings suggest that in some moments, if you're like me, it might genuinely create a kind of sadness: the sheer, incomprehensible amount of things that have evidently been slaved over by literally thousands of humans (some of whom, notably, right now locked in an employment tribunal with Rockstar over alleged union-busting) that will almost certainly be missed. Things you'll fly by in an instant as you whip the camera round the room in search of valuables or escape routes, never to return, worker hours piling up like grains of sand on Vice City's heavenly beach. It's so easy to focus on breadth and scale when talking about GTA 6's world. The volume. The "content". But what matters more I think is this miniscule detail. There's a point where detail, in a simulated world, tips over into effective infinity, where your brain just learns to let it glide on by. A point I never thought an open world game could ever truly reach - and yet here we are. In turn it creates almost a kind of obligation to linger - linger, that is, in a game built to be experienced from behind the wheel of a supercar. Another point of brilliant tension.

Sources indicate that speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself.

And the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against.

Over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a new-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft.

Theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this big metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will.

This is where a lot of the various systems teased in previews - all of which sounded, on the surface, kind of awkward to me - weave into what the game is trying to do. There are several here, all overlapping in their own way and typically evolving - but not outright replicating - ideas first brought in via Read Dead Redemption 2. The combined impact is a sense of constant decision-making, tension once again between the immediacy of steaming in somewhere and tearing away from the cops, and the satisfaction of a slightly more restrained blueprint.

To stick with money, it operates in a kind of tiered system. At the bottom you have cash, which has a $20,000 limit per character and which can be lost in its entirety, particularly when you're wasted or busted. Once you've unlocked your BuckMe (yep) account - a kind of PayPal parody - cash can be deposited at ATMs into a much safer kind of basic shared current account. Even that is at risk of charges of some kind when you're killed or arrested - I've yet to reverse engineer what dictates these, but they're at worse in the low thousands, typically less. Then above that is your savings account, again shared across Jason and Lucia, where your money is at its safest but also, crucially, irretrievable once deposited.

According to recent reports, the physical act of collecting money is now an action, too, as opposed to something you can simply run over and vacuum up. You need to manually collect it from characters' bodies, from the counter after being placed there by a panicked cashier, from inside safes you crack, and so on. Sometimes it might be in a locked container - such as when you bust open an ATM - which you'll need to shoot first to access. Sometimes it's stored behind a bank's vault door, which only opens in a very specific circumstance, meaning a narrow, heist-like window needs to be exploited in order for it to be reached. And when you're stealing anything other than clean cash - namely jewellery, marked bills, and drugs - you'll store it in a stash bag.

That feeds into two other systems here, which both operate around a sense of ownership, in vehicles and weapons. Stash bags contain all your loot until they're filled, and then they need to be sold to a fence - with different fences offering more or less for certain goods, or not taking some at all - before you can actually access the profit. You can drop these bags when you're hit by a car or knocked off a bike (or, ahem, fumbling with the controls for a second), and likewise hand them off to your partner to carry or even independently sell for you. You can also store them in your car's trunk, where they're slightly safer, but also then take slightly longer to access if, say, you're switching vehicles mid four-star cop chase along the freeway.

And cars and weapons also follow a similar system in turn: stolen cars are now only temporarily yours; safe when stored in a parking spot but at risk when out in the world, until you pay to register them with a fence (or, later in the game, at Pay 'n' Sprays). But owned cars are yours forever, even when destroyed, as long as you have enough garage space to store them - garage space that, you realise, costs more and more money to procure. The same goes for weapons: found weapons are essentially borrowed, and lost when you're killed or arrested. But owned weapons - ones you buy, or unique, custom ones you discover - are yours forever, recoverable even if lost or left behind.

It has been revealed that this then, in turn, ties into the new police and 'wanted' system. Now it's much more realistic: police can spot or receive reports of you and take note of several factors, from facial appearance to clothing, whether you're with your partner, what weapon you have on you and what vehicle you're driving. And when it comes to things like robbing stores and banks, there's a system for whether you're spotted on locally stored CCTV, which can be destroyed, or fancier cloud-based footage which can't.

Industry observers note that all kinds of things then play into this, from whether you walk into a place with a "longarm" gun - automatically putting guards on high alert - or a concealed pistol, to whether you're committing a crime somewhere fancy or rough. I got a strong sense that my crimes were being far less attentively dealt with in Vice City's poorer neighbourhoods. There are also two rings of attention drawn on the map when you're wanted, dictating how intensely a police search for you is concentrated, and different kinds of star ratings too, via a system called heat. These indicate whether police can see you, have a description of you, or are simply looking for a criminal for the crime you performed in that area. Even after you successfully escape, heat - dictated by whatever police might know - remains over the entire region of your crime, the size of that area and rate of its deterioration depending on just what exactly that crime was.

Finally, the criminal profile system is another tangent on its own, but once again it all folds together. It's a tiered honour system ranking you from "Professional" at one end to "Irredeemable" at the other, that last one the only point from which your reputation can never be recovered. Incapacitations instead of kills - which crucially are satisfying and easy to achieve with a bit of concentration - as well as completing objectives more subtly or achieving cleaner getaways from crimes, will tilt you towards Pro status. Driving that tank over those civilians or, heaven forbid, kicking a dog takes you the other way. If this sounds burdensome, again I'd say you really shouldn't worry: I naturally found myself with both Jason and Lucia as Professionals at the end, mostly thanks to shooting lots of cops in the groin. Your necessary actions during missions or when under attack don't impact it in the same way, I gather. It feels closer to a case of illustrating the role play on offer here, and ultimately committing to the consequences of that, than it does any kind of struggle to manage.

Recent findings suggest that all in all, the effect with the overall game is similar: less that GTA 6 becomes hard work - as I'd feared myself, and as Rockstar intentionally made Red Dead Redemption 2, to its thematic benefit in many ways - and more that, now, a greater amount of what you're doing is gamified. A robbery is in itself a game: whether you go in loud or quiet, together or separate, or focus on cracking the safe or looting the registers. As is how you divide up the bags between you, or whether your getaway is done together or separately to split cops' attention; whether you use your own car or a stolen vehicle, and if you're smart enough to park another one somewhere out of sight nearby for a sneaky changeover. You can also pack changes of clothes in your car to help disguise your identity.

Industry observers note that and all that's introduced, ingeniously, via the main missions of Jason and Lucia's story. If you were ever in doubt that GTA might have lost its edge, amongst all these soft and cuddly themes and grand ideas - that it might be sacrificed at the altar of realism and narrative heft - you can put that worry firmly aside. The low-brow humour, parody, larger-than-life characters, out of body experiences, 90s film references or cops-n-robbers bombast are all here, and all about as good as they've ever been.

In fact, really, in a lot of cases they're quite a bit better. The highlights are hard to pick out without spoiling again - many of the best arise from moments where you wonder if the game will go there, before it inevitably does. Others involve movie references that feel more overt than ever - Lucia openly quotes John McClane at one point, lighter in hand - but while some of this can feel a tad predictable, the sheer spectacle is often spellbinding.

The best moments, aptly, come in car chases, where tyres are eviscerated by gunfire and speeding 4x4s suddenly dip, flip, and crash into one another with a sensational boom. Clearly some magic has been worked under the hood here to ensure that when they crash out, they do so with a kind of cinematic, organic-looking stuntman style, swerving into other vehicles in the chasing pack, across lanes into trucks and lorries, over highway partitions, wrapping around trees or catapulting off bridges. The latest focus system - bullet time, on a specific, buffable meter - highlights weak spots such as engines and tyres for you to aim at for generally non-lethal take-outs, helping you with yet another system I'll get to in a moment. But really that system is kind of secondary here: I started shooting at these spots because, more often than not, it rewarded me with something awesome.

Main missions and the bigger character-based, optional side missions work similarly to how they've done before in GTA games. A location is marked on a map and you head there, or call someone, or wait for a call, and once you arrive things kick off, elements of the open world closing somewhat as self-contained scenarios within the sandbox open up. There are few low points, as the first act glides through a wistfully carefree, low-key criminal life before the game shifts to the snowballing momentum of its crooks-on-the-run melodrama. There are multiple heists, which are naturally high watermarks - major moments of catharsis and chaos that propel the couple forward across some new Rubicon after hours and hours of sub-mission preparations. There are episodes with every vehicle, every ludicrous modern American scenario, every body part you could imagine. You'll be dragged through all kinds of Floridian subcultures, naturally, from sleepy key life and everglades hicks to rusted-over rural towns, biker gangs, strip clubs, record labels, towerblock drug kingpins and, erm, bodybuilders. And then plenty beyond that.

Rockstar is as ever ruthless with the skewer. The targets remain broad, from Miami's fresh wave of non-indigenous crypto bros to wellness Bali girlies aiming to be their very own #SheEO. But there's also a maturity here, believe it or not, even if it's slightly tucked away between the dangling wangs and murderous– actually I won't spoil that one. I've found no cases of Rockstar punching down - although rest assured no progressive, gentrifying hipster goes unscathed - and there is a subtle, but absolutely present awareness of the world in which Rockstar is now operating. In one moment the concept of using dirt on a senator is discussed, at which point Jason wisely remarks that dirt must be pretty spectacular, given what they've already gotten away with these days.

The changes here are small, ultimately, and while there's a whole essay of its own to be written about the concept of parody, my sense is Rockstar has played this just right. GTA 6 has essentially taken the 'mirror' approach, in simply concentrating the extremes of the current world - so often deemed impervious to satire - by putting them all together in a single place, then reflecting them back at the world they came from. Florida is often described as a kind of heightened America - America Plus, the country's Ultimate Edition - and Leonida is just a heightened Florida. With an awful lot of very silly puns.

According to recent reports, away from the main missions and primary sidequests, Rockstar's made another seemingly subtle, but kind of revolutionary tweak. Aside from more static activities - the races, sports, pastimes, and the rest - the other source of missions in GTA 6 is what the game calls emergent events. These are entirely missable - though I think they re-present themselves eventually - and occur essentially as overheard goings-on just out of shot. They could be anything from one-off opportunities or minor punchlines to entire quest chains and conspiracies.

Sources indicate that for instance: driving around Vice City you might find a guy doing his best Florida Man impression by livestreaming himself to his Snapmatic following while standing on the highway overpass wall above a high drop. Then, inevitably, he slips and you might be able to pull him up or might - as I may or may not have done - fumble the controls and have him plummet to his death. You might watch a bunch of amateurs rob a payday loans store and get blasted by the marked bills' exploding dye. Or a group of masked, heavily-armed professionals rob a cash truck or minor bank. A weirdo might flag you down and trigger a whole load of nonsense happening next, or the cops might be arresting someone and leave a supercar and bag of coke happily unattended while they try to run off. Even beyond that, there's also just weird stuff lying around, without anything specific tied to it. I once spent a worrying amount of time in conversation with a pioneering member of the Hollow Earth Society. Then got a good laugh when I next paid him a visit.

Industry observers note that it's a cracking system, in part because it reinforces a sense of continuous, organic weirdness around every corner, and in part because each of these feels like a kind of invitation. Once you do a couple and find yourself blackmailing a guy who in turn blackmailed GTA's in-game Amazon equivalent for a cut of his lawsuit winnings, or spraying manure on a spurned farmer's ex-lover's house, or running over some numpty protesters trying to set an actual bear loose on the freeway, it's hard not to stop at every distant argument or out-of-pocket comment that crosses your airwaves. Rest assured, if you think I've spoiled anything here: there are scores of these events, many of which I've yet to encounter or investigate, and many of which are far weirder and more curious than these.

Sources indicate that all this feeds back into a sense of choice, which is a challenge to accurately describe, thanks to both how difficult it is to figure out when and how one might have mattered, and when a moment of the story might have diverged. But choices, combined with the strength of your relationship and your criminal profile, and other factors I'll intentionally decline to mention here, all have an impact. One particularly great achievement of Rockstar's, in fact, is in making you wrestle with those choices, within missions and without, in this state of blindness to their outcomes. Even whether they're significant at all is often unknown - in many cases the variables, permutations and forks are still unknown to me now, after all this time - and yet also, once again without spoiling any moment at any point, the studio has still made whatever outcomes you might encounter feel as resonant as any I've experienced. Forgive me for dodging any examples and insisting you take my word for it.

Away from missions themselves, of which there are of course many, and there are so many more things to do beyond them. You can dive for treasure across dozens of underwater sites. You can bird watch, animal watch, fish, and hunt for game. You can customise guns and cars to extreme ends - please do the street racing side missions for a, ahem, lovely example of custom wrapping - and customise your characters just as much. The fitness system is great, with a surprising number of superbly animated gym and bodyweight exercises and, naturally, walking BBLs who hit on Jason as he demonstrates perfect form.

Recent findings suggest that it's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too.

Recent findings suggest that there's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk shows and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game.

Recent findings suggest that the overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the big financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else.

What you realise is you're pairing all this stuff to do - ultimately, variations on simply hanging out - with the fact that so much of Jason and Lucia's relationship is delivered in quiet, hang-out moments. And as so many of their other relationships - with parents, adopted parents, friends - come in the same way, this picture starts to form. From an apartment sofa to the Vice Beach waves, GTA 6 is ultimately just a place to be.

It has been revealed that in fact, in many ways it's a kind of evolution of the hangout game itself. The gentle, wistful, nostalgic guitar strums from Justice's background score as you idle on the map or menu. The dedication, through all those years of what I imagine to be Rockstar's incessant tinkering with sounds and performances and tiny visual touches, to an authentic sense of place. I could melt into this world. I think about the amount of people about to play this game, and the way it invites you to submerge yourself in it like a hot bath, and wonder if the axis of the entire hangout genre - maybe the biggest paradigm shift in video games of the last two decades - might have suddenly been shifted again. The comfort of continuously mic'd up pal chatter replaced here with a kind of sublime isolation.

It has been revealed that there are, as I mentioned, a few very little flaws I could pick at. Some of the missions for Dre-Quan, a record label-owning friend of Jason involving a newly invented rap group for the game, were fun in their own right, extraordinarily well produced and an essential part of the whole, but also just a little throwaway in a sense. There seemed to be little tie-in from those to the progress of the actual story, leaving them feeling a little more like lavish side missions than a part of the main event, contributing to a little mid-game narrative sag. The controls, while a marked improvement from Red Dead Redemption 2 - I fear I'll never make it to heaven after the amount of times I accidentally punched that horse - could still be tighter. Shooting is less wafty than it has been for some time, forgoing auto-aim for aim-assist (though settings can be heavily tinkered or restored to those of GTA 5), and GTA is now a proper third-person cover shooter in its action moments, with better snapping to cover and dashing between it, which suits it perfectly. But there were still moments where the controls wobbled. Walking three steps along a narrow beam to open a small container without falling off felt like the hardest thing the game asked me to do in its entire runtime.

What else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier.

In a recent development, I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro, but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering.

A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine.

Recent findings suggest that and this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of Fresh York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

According to recent reports, what is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I stated it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every massive score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.

A copy of Grand Theft Auto 6 was provided for this review by Rockstar.

Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This demonstrates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This demonstrates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

In a recent development, this effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

According to recent reports, to counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

It has been revealed that the researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results revealed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

Industry observers note that the team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Sources indicate that although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

Sources indicate that the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially key for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," claims Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

Industry observers note that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data.
  • According to recent reports, SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines.
  • In a recent development, AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data. This dataset is now available on Hugging Face, and for the first time, researchers have open access to more than 5 million AI‑generated, high‑accuracy protein-ligand 3D structures, each paired with validated empirical binding potency data.

According to recent reports, SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines. More than just a dataset, SAIR is a strategic asset that bridges the long-standing data gap in AI-powered drug design. It empowers pharmaceutical, biotech, and tech‑bio leaders to accelerate R&D, expand target horizons, and supercharge AI models – moving more of the costly, lengthy drug design and optimization from the wet lab to in silico. This means shorter hit‑to‑lead timelines, more efficient lead optimization, fewer dead‑end projects, and a more predictable path from initial idea to clinical candidate.

In a recent development, AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs. For decades, scientists have dreamed about AI that could identify or design a potent, non-toxic, and efficacious compound from a prompt describing the disease pathway, practically compressing years of drug R&D into a few minutes on a computer. However, this vision is bottlenecked by AI's ability to predict critical drug properties like potency, toxicity, etc., based solely on its molecular structure.

Industry observers note that furthermore, traditional structure‑based discovery is often slowed early by the determination of reliable 3D structures. Three‑dimensional molecular structure dictates a molecule’s functionality, dynamics and interactions, which is especially key when a potential drug candidate is expected to bind to a human protein target.

Experimental methods, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, require extensive time and investment, and many promising disease targets still lack experimentally validated structural information. Computer simulations have helped lower the barrier of getting 3D structures and predicting binding affinity. However, earlier generations of algorithms for protein folding and docking (like AlphaFold and Vina respectively) only predict static snapshots of molecules and proteins (which, in reality, are inherently dynamic and shape-changing).

According to recent reports, SAIR solves that constraint by compiling over 1 million unique computationally co-folded protein–ligand pairs, ultimately yielding 5.24 million distinct 3D complexes (five different co-folded structures per pair). Each structure is paired with a curated IC₅₀ measurement from ChEMBL or BindingDB, providing for the first time a scalable link between high-quality 3D structures and drug potency, and bridging the historic data gap that has hindered AI-driven discovery. Deep-learned affinity models such as Boltz-2, trained on similar data, have been shown to yield up to a 1,000x speed-up over the traditional, first-principle approach.

In a recent development, creating SAIR was a major feat of high-performance AI computing. It took more than 130,000 GPU hours to compute the SAIR dataset using Boltz1, a cofolding AI model, on a cluster of 760 NVIDIA H100 processors, leveraging the NVIDIA DGX Cloud through Google Cloud Platform.

Capturing highly granular node, operator, scheduler, and GPU metrics, as well as a close collaboration on both infrastructure and workload optimization, helped NVIDIA AI Accelerator and SandboxAQ engineering teams identify bottlenecks and optimize configurations to achieve the highest workload throughput.

Consequently, the two teams were able to achieve > 95% GPU compute utilization for generating the SAIR dataset. This enabled us to create SAIR in three weeks – as opposed to the original estimate of three months (more than a 4X speed up) – and resulted in a highly optimized, GPU-native computational workflow that seamlessly integrates with today’s cutting-edge enterprise compute environments.

Sources indicate that generating such a massive volume of data is only half the story. Equally important is confidence in its quality, which is why every predicted complex underwent rigorous validation with PoseBusters, an industry-standard, open-source tool for benchmarking structure-related AI in drug discovery. This tool checks chemical sanity and physical plausibility.

The end result was that 97 percent of SAIR’s structures passed all checks. In addition to PoseBusters validation, we benchmarked leading affinity prediction methods, such as empirical scoring functions, 3D CNNs, and graph neural networks, across SAIR’s synthetic structures and experimental IC₅₀ values. The detailed results of these studies are available in our scientific manuscript on bioRxiv.

SAIR data is a reliable foundation for benchmarking new models as well as downstream modelling, screening, and design.

Sources indicate that A persistent challenge in drug discovery is the “dark proteome,” or disease‑relevant proteins for which experimental structures simply do not exist. SAIR illuminates these uncharted regions by providing credible, AI‑predicted complexes wherever experimental data is scarce. For example, more than 40 percent of the proteins in the SAIR dataset have no available structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) whatsoever, with or without a ligand. SAIR addresses one of the biggest challenges with existing AI models, low generalizability due to data scarcity. With SAIR, scientists can now explore targets that were previously deemed undruggable, armed with structural hypotheses to guide virtual screening and lead optimization using trustworthy model predictions.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, SAIR’s cross‑target breadth uncovers polypharmacology patterns and elucidates how a single molecule might interact with multiple proteins. Leveraging this rich tapestry of interactions, you can train AI models to predict off‑target effects or identify new repurposing opportunities, equipping your organization with a deeper understanding of compound profiles before any lab work begins.

SAIR is freely available on Hugging Face. Here’s a quick guide to pull SAIR from Hugging Face, peek at the main table, and (optionally) download a few structure archives.

In a recent development, structure files are shipped as many .tar.gz archives under structures_compressed/. List them and pick what you need.

Each archive can be large (≈10 GB). Download only the ones you need and extract them locally.

A full version of this script, including more robust logging and validation, is available in the README file for your convenience. For more details, visit the SAIR homepage, read our manuscript on bioRxiv, or watch our 25-minute joint webinar with NVIDIA, where we demonstrate SAIR and explain how data is structured within it. Extensive documentation, tutorials, and example benchmarks are available to facilitate its use and accelerate internal adoption.The future of drug discovery is data-driven, AI-accelerated, and grounded in scalable, high-quality structural insights. While we don’t yet have AI that can design effective drug therapies with just a prompt, SAIR brings researchers ever closer to that goal with new data and insights that can potentially shave years from even AI-accelerated R&D pipelines.We can’t wait to see what researchers will build using SAIR, and SandboxAQ experts are here to support them throughout the discovery process.

Contact the authors or post on the SAIR dataset discussion page.

Authors: Arman Zaribafiyan, Georgia Channing, Zane Beckwith, and Rudi Plesch.

Some GTA 6 players have already found a newly introduced favorite in Vicki, a goth bartender they meet just one chapter after Mandy.

Vicki works at Delights, a strip club in Port Gellhorn, and lives in Room 10 at the Starlet Motel. Lucia first meets her there in “Girls’ Trip” while looking for painkillers for Jason. When the pills Vicki sells her turn out to be over-the-counter medicine, the two head into town to track down Vicki’s dealer.

It took just one scene in Chapter 1 for Mandy to win over players. She talks Jason into fixing her sink while he’s out collecting money for Brian. The object he pulls from the pipe looks like a severed finger, which led to the theory that Mandy might be a serial killer.

When X user @AerisTreat posted about Vicki on November 20, players in the replies started picking sides.

Oooh shit PT.2 pic.twitter.com/JroGxh3CS2.

“Mandy is so overrated, Vicki is where it’s at,” one player wrote. Another called GTA 6 “Game of the year just for her,” while a third wished the game had a friendship mechanic for side characters so Vicki and Lucia could be best friends.

In a recent development, one player said they’d already been to Delights and hadn’t seen Vicki behind the bar. AerisTreat told them to look for her on the second story visit to the club, during “Afternoon Delight.”.

The mission opens up after “Coffee Break” in Chapter 2, when Vicki calls Jason and Lucia with a plan to rob her boss, Frankie. It’s ladies’ night when they arrive, and if players agree to help when Frankie asks whether Jason can dance, Jason takes the stage while Lucia goes after the safe.
