📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the decade or so since Grand Theft Auto Online's arrival, its roads have become a kind of home; well-loved by its racers, its gear heads, and speed freaks. It's a game that allows players to lose themselves in the roleplay, the heists, and the crime sprees. But for me, an occasional dipper into its major updates, the car folk have always been the engine driving its appeal.

So when the GTA Online community decided to host Last Ride events this week - a sort of mass in-game road trip and a communal farewell before attention inevitably turned to GTA 6 - I was keen to join in. The Last Drive was scheduled to begin an hour before GTA 6's launch, and would see numerous groups embarking on their own journey across GTA Online's servers, all taking the same route: starting at Los Santos' Del Perro Pier and following the highway around Los Santos' entire perimeter before finally rolling up to its airport. Players would then fly off into the sunset, close the game, and move on. Some just for a while, others perhaps forever.

In a recent development, kirsty is one of the many long-time players who chose to embark on their own last drive as part of the event. She runs the Fast Crew racing community in GTA Online and has been playing since the beginning in 2013, even meeting her fiance through the game. Unlike some, however, she plans to stick around in GTA Online after GTA 6's release, at least until the fresh game's equivalent comes along.

It's the social dynamic of GTA Online that makes it special, Kirsty tells me when we speak online, and she calls it a community of players "that thrives from supporting each other, racing together and just having fun". She points to GTA Online's 30-player sessions as one reason for its enduring appeal "That's crucial for people in communities like ours," she explains. "Gaming is an escape to many people, a distraction or a coping method. GTA is special because it stayed alive for so long, giving people that escape.".

Then there's Brittany, who leads the GTA Online Ascent racing community. Brittany has a real-life kart racing background, and built race tracks across various Xbox 360 games before arriving in GTA Online. As with many of the players I spoke with, the in-game connections Brittany made have blossomed into real-life friendships, all built around racing.

"GTA Online introduced me to many lifelong friends," they explain. "Hell, I even met my girlfriend Ari through the GTA Racing community. Every year, five-to-six of us go to the Indy 500 and all of us met through my [GTA Online] PC racing community BRITCAR." Brittany was also planning their own Last Drive, using old cars from the game's earlier years.

It's clear GTA Online has become more than just a game to many people, and I was eager to see how players might choose to say goodbye. So as GTA 6 loomed, I booted up GTA Online and prepared for my own Last Drive, waiting near the pier in a random online lobby. Slowly, other people started to arrive - all seemingly strangers - and at the allotted time, we slowly began making our way around the map as one.

What I saw was brilliant. A snaking line of customised cars, custom paint jobs, and underlighting, slowly navigating the island; a peaceful, reverential convoy of players who weren't blasting away at each other with weapons for once. The chaos of the typical GTA Online lobby never broke out. Instead, there was a sort of unspoken armistice between those eager to enjoy one last moment in a game they'd spent so much time in. Gradually, more people joined our conga line.

Besides being a lovely way to close a chapter for many, it allowed for a cheeky bit of peacocking too. Many players pulled up in truly exceptional rides: there were supercars, bulky muscle cars, and street-racer lightshows, all as much an expression of their owners' personalities and tastes as any human avatar.

At one point, the leader of this snaking pack made a wrong turn, taking us into a dockyard and an unfortunate dead-end. We then all had to slowly reverse out - a time-consuming, if amusing, process which allowed one opportunistic spectator to pull up and take a few of us out with a well-placed RPG. But after we'd all reconvened nearby, the respectful atmosphere resumed. No flying Oppressor Mk II rained missiles on us, and there weren't any kamikaze crashes interrupting our final drive.

Recent findings suggest that when we did finally reach the airport, people left their vehicles and things took a more knockabout turn. Together we huddled for a few moments, letting off gunfire and fireworks into the night. Then the cops came, and the group rushed to steal planes and helicopters before things got wilder still.

Slowly, eventually our group began to disperse. Players either went on to cause some final havoc before GTA 6's arrival, or they did as I did, flying over the ocean into the sunset before leaving the server once and for all. It sounds sappy but it was moving. Here, a game perhaps best known for its player-versus-player hijinks had - thanks to a close-knit community consisting of people like Kirsty, Brittany, and all their friends - became a wholesome drive along. A send off to the game as it was, before ushering in a upcoming dawn.

According to recent reports, it speaks to what is special about GTA Online, really. A playground people have spent years in, clearly still notable to them, and a chance to say a farewell of sorts from the place they feel most comfortable: behind the wheel.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads.

Industry observers note that in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

Recent findings suggest that the decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

It has been revealed that kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

However, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

According to recent reports, in our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

This does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

In our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

Kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The notable point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

According to recent reports, removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

The resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

That distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Industry observers note that our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

Industry observers note that other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

In a recent development, A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

Industry observers note that NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address proposal, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not notable.

An overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are vital. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

Recent findings suggest that the broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

Industry observers note that as more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

Sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

It has been revealed that if most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

Latest Update: mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages.
  • If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!
  • mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages. It indicates significant performance and speed improvements over previous multilingual models, being the first to improve upon XLM-R, while also developing new strategies for effectively learning low-resource languages. mmBERT builds upon ModernBERT for a blazingly fast architecture, and adds novel components to enable efficient multilingual learning.

If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!

mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases. The foundation of our training data consists of three primary open-source and high-quality web crawls that enable both multilingual coverage and data quality:.

It has been revealed that DCLM and Filtered DCLM provides the highest quality English content available, serving as the backbone for strong English performance (with the filtered data coming from Dolmino). This dataset represents state-of-the-art web filtering techniques and forms a crucial component. Due to the high quality of this data, we use a signficantly higher proportion of English than previous generation multilingual encoder models (up to 18%).

Industry observers note that fineWeb2 delivers broad multilingual web content covering over 1,800 languages. This dataset enables our extensive multilingual coverage while maintaining reasonable quality standards across diverse language families and scripts.

FineWeb2-HQ consists of a filtered subset of FineWeb2 focusing on 20 high-resource languages. This filtered version provides higher-quality multilingual content that bridges the gap between English-only filtered data and broad multilingual coverage.

The training data also incorporates specialized corpora from Dolma, MegaWika v2, ProLong and more: code repositories (StarCoder, ProLong), academic content (ArXiv, PeS2o), reference materials (Wikipedia, textbooks), and community discussions (StackExchange), along with instruction and mathematical datasets.

The key innovation in our data approach is the progressive language inclusion strategy shown in Figure 1. At each phase we progressively sample from a flatter distribution (i.e. closer to uniform), while also adding newly introduced languages. This means that high resource languages like Russian start off with a high percentage of the data (i.e. 9%) and then in the last phase of training end around half of that. We start with 60 high-resource languages during pre-training, expand to 110 languages during mid-training, and finally include all 1,833 languages from FineWeb2 during the decay phase. This allows us to maximize the impact of limited low-resource language data without excess reptitions and while maintaining high overall data quality.

mmBERT builds upon the ModernBERT architecture but introduces several key innovations for multilingual learning:.

Sources indicate that we use the same core architecture as ModernBERT-base with 22 layers and 1152 intermediate dimensions, but switch to the Gemma 2 tokenizer to better handle multilingual text. The base model has 110M non-embedding parameters (307M total due to the larger vocabulary), while the small variant has 42M non-embedding parameters (140M total).

Our training follows a carefully designed three-phase schedule:.

In a recent development, inverse Mask Ratio Schedule: Instead of using a fixed masking rate, we progressively reduce the mask ratio from 30% → 15% → 5% across training phases. This allows the model to learn basic representations with higher masking early on, then focus on more nuanced understanding with lower masking rates.

Annealed Language Learning: We dynamically adjust the temperature for multilingual data sampling from τ=0.7 → 0.5 → 0.3. This creates a progression from high-resource language bias toward more uniform sampling, enabling the model to build a strong multilingual foundation before learning low-resource languages.

Sources indicate that progressive Language Addition: Rather than training on all languages simultaneously, we strategically add languages at each phase (60 → 110 → 1,833). This maximizes learning efficiency by avoiding excessive epochs on limited low-resource data while still achieving strong performance.

Model Merging: We train three different variants during the decay phase (English-focused, 110-language, and all-language) and use TIES merging to combine their strengths into the final model.

English Performance: On the English GLUE benchmark (Table 1), mmBERT base achieves strong performance, substantially outperforming other multilingual models like XLM-R (multilingual RoBERTa) base and mGTE base, while remaining competitive to English-only models despite less than 25% of the mmBERT training data being English.

It has been revealed that multilingual Performance: mmBERT shows significant improvements on XTREME benchmark compared to XLM-R as demonstrated in Table 2. Notable gains include strong performance on XNLI classification, substantial improvements in question answering tasks like TyDiQA, and competitive results across PAWS-X and XCOPA for cross-lingual understanding.

The model performs well across most categories, with the exception of some structured prediction tasks like NER and POS tagging, likely due to tokenizer differences that affect word boundary detection. On these categories, it performs about the same as the previous generation, but can be applied to more languages.

English Retrieval: Even though mmBERT is designed for massively multilingual settings, in the MTEB v2 English benchmarks (Table 3), mmBERT indicates significant gains over previous multilingual models and even ties the capabilities of English-only models like ModernBERT!

Multilingual Retrieval: mmBERT reveals consistent improvements on MTEB v2 multilingual benchmarks compared to other models (Table 4).

Sources indicate that code Retrieval: Due to the modern tokenizer (based on Gemma 2) mmBERT also reveals strong coding performance (Table 5), making mmBERT suitable for any type of textual data. The only model that outperforms it is EuroBERT, which was able to use the non-publicly accessible Stack v2 dataset.

Recent findings suggest that one of mmBERT's most significant novel features is demonstrating that low-resource languages can be effectively learned during the short decay phase of training. We validated this approach by testing on languages only introduced during the final 100B token decay phase.

Dramatic Performance Gains: Testing on TiQuaD (Tigrinya) and FoQA (Faroese), we observed substantial improvements when these languages were included in the decay phase, as shown in Figure 2. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our progressive language learning approach.

In a recent development, competitive with Large Models: Despite only seeing these languages in the final training phase, mmBERT achieves performance levels that exceed much larger models. On Faroese question answering where LLMs have been benchmarked, mmBERT outperforms Google Gemini 2.5 Pro and OpenAI o3.

Recent findings suggest that rapid Learning Mechanism: The success of decay-phase language learning stems from the model's ability to leverage its strong multilingual foundation built during earlier phases. When exposed to newly introduced languages, the model can quickly adapt existing cross-lingual representations rather than learning from scratch.

Model Merging Benefits: The final mmBERT models successfully retain most of the decay-phase improvements while benefiting from the English-focused and high-resource variants through TIES merging.

mmBERT delivers substantial efficiency gains over previous multilingual encoder models through architectural improvements inherited from ModernBERT:.

Industry observers note that throughput Performance: mmBERT processes text significantly faster than existing multilingual models across various sequence lengths, as demonstrated in Figure 3. Both the small and base models show substantial speed improvements over previous multilingual encoders.

Modern Architecture Benefits: The efficiency gains come from two main technical improvements:.

Sequence Length Scaling: Unlike older models limited to 512 tokens, mmBERT handles up to 8,192 tokens efficiently while maintaining high throughput. This makes it suitable for longer document processing tasks that are increasingly common in multilingual applications.

Energy Efficiency: The combination of better throughput and modern architecture results in lower computational costs for inference, making mmBERT more practical for production deployments where multilingual support is needed at scale.

These efficiency improvements make mmBERT not just more accurate than previous multilingual encoders, but also significantly more practical for real usage.

You can use these models with just a few lines of code!

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • Recent findings suggest that but position and time are different.
  • The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

Recent findings suggest that but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

According to recent reports, understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

In a recent development, at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

Industry observers note that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Recent findings suggest that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

It has been revealed that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a latest laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Industry observers note that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It indicated that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

It has been revealed that what makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Recent findings suggest that their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

In a recent development, for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

Industry observers note that the team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

Sources indicate that in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

It has been revealed that the findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Industry observers note that transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists upcoming ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

It has been revealed that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

Industry observers note that "In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

According to recent reports, that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a fresh foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

In a recent development, for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

Tech Report: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," notes Yiwen Chu.

It has been revealed that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

Industry observers note that the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an crucial role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Recent findings suggest that chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

According to recent reports, quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are right now beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Industry observers note that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

According to recent reports, another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Latest Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

Recent findings suggest that the research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Industry observers note that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

In a recent development, to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two key computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

In a recent development, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Recent findings suggest that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

One of the most significant findings is that the fresh system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Industry observers note that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Industry observers note that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#103644. Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells.
  • In a recent development, while large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks. The goal of the Jupyter Agent is to give the model the ultimate tool: code execution.

Recent findings suggest that A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells. So we built Jupyter Agent to act as an agent that can execute code directly inside a Jupyter notebook and use this environment to solve data analysis and data science tasks. Think of it like Cursor, but living natively inside your data science workflow.We built a demo of this vision with Qwen-3 Coder, presently one of the strongest coding models. This is a follow-up to our earlier work on jupyter-agent (v1).

In a recent development, while large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them. To this end, we focus on strengthening smaller models to perform well on agentic data science tasks as they presently struggle to compete with the large models.

The goal of this project is to build a pipeline to first generate high-quality training data, then fine-tune an existing small model, and finally evaluate whether the model's performance improves on relevant benchmarks.

Let’s begin with the last step: selecting a strong benchmark for evaluating models on data science tasks.

In order to understand if we are making progress towards better data science agents we need a benchmark to measure such capabilities. Last year, in partnership with Adyen, we introduced the DABStep benchmark: a way to evaluate data science agents on realistic tasks. The setup is simple: provide the LLM with datasets and ask it to answer non-trivial data questions.

Industry observers note that this benchmark remains challenging for today’s LLMs — e.g. the best out-of-the-box model is Claude 4 Sonnet which reaches not even 20% accuracy on the hard tasks.You can explore the live leaderboard here.

It has been revealed that now that we identified a good benchmark we can try to climb it! We set out to build a dataset for fine-tuning such that even a small data agent model could perform well on DABStep.

Our first choice was Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507: extremely small (fast to iterate with, easy to run), yet strong enough to act in agentic scenarios.

It has been revealed that not great — but a promising starting point, since it left a lot of room for improvement. Let's see how we can improve it!

A core aspect of agents that sets it apart from a pure chat model is the scaffolding built around the model to steer its behaviour. The evaluation script in DABStep for example uses smolagents to execute code. Smolagents comes with predefined behaviors, prompting structures, and expected formats.

We also studied the Qwen-Agent codebase, where the authors tailoring scaffolding to the model. This makes sense: Claude Code, for example, works shockingly well with Claude Sonnet because their scaffolding is aligned.

So, we restructured our scaffolding:.

Results: accuracy jumped from 44.4% → 59.7% (easy split). 🚀.

With simplified scaffolding in place, we focused on fine-tuning Qwen3-4B for data science agentic tasks.

The recipe to improve a model on a certain task or behaviour is to train it on data that reflects the tasks as closely as possible. A natural starting point is to look at real Jupyter Notebooks and find notebooks that align closely with the task that we plan to tackle, namely data analysis.

Kaggle notebooks offer a wealth of high quality data analysis notebooks and are made available by Kaggle:.

Industry observers note that now that we have good results with a base model it's time to build a dataset that will help us improve it even further. We designed a multi-stage pipeline using Datatrove to clean and prepare Kaggle notebooks at scale.

We started with ~2TB of Kaggle notebooks and reduced it to ~250GB reusing our work from the BigCode project. As part of the StarCoder2 training data processing the notebooks (without output cells) were already deduplicated. Most Kaggle notebooks are small variations or near-identical copies, so this step was essential.Key insight: ~90% of raw notebooks are duplicates, which would have skewed training if left unfiltered.

Most Kaggle notebooks reference external datasets via Kaggle metadata. To make sure the code inside notebooks could actually run, we built a pipeline that automatically fetched these linked datasets. This step was crucial, since many notebooks would otherwise be incomplete or non-executable.

Recent findings suggest that using the kagglehub package, we downloaded thousands of datasets — about 5TB in total. To keep things manageable and relevant:.

By the end, we had a rich collection of executable notebooks paired with their datasets, providing the foundation for training agents in realistic, runnable environments.

Recent findings suggest that we scored notebooks based on educational quality using Qwen3-32B. We saw that using the whole notebook was not optimal, as many contained trivial or broken code. Our educational scoring approach is detailed in edu_scoring.py.

TL;DR: We assigned each notebook a score from 1–5 based on clarity, completeness, and educational value, and kept only those above a chosen threshold. This filtering removed about 70% of the notebooks.

Industry observers note that this is similar to the insight from the BeyondWeb paper, which revealed that using high-quality data is better for synthetic data generation — a step we relied on for QA (Question-Answer) generation. This helped the model learn from “high quality” notebooks instead of noisy ones.

Industry observers note that we excluded notebooks about training LLMs or unrelated to data analysis. We also removed notebooks that didn’t actually use datasets through an automated LLM-based filtering process using Qwen3-32B. The implementation of filtering can be found in extract_packages_and_files.py.

Sources indicate that TL;DR: We prompted Qwen3-32B to identify and remove notebooks that either (1) had nothing to do with data analysis, or (2) didn’t actually use datasets. This step removed about 20% of the notebooks.

This ensured we trained only on relevant data science tasks.

Using the cleaned notebooks, we generated question–answer pairs using Qwen3-32B. The questions and answer are grounded in the real notebook traces so the QA pairs are based on real code execution results. Prompt design: we asked the LLM to produce natural questions that could realistically be asked of the dataset, then validated whether the notebook provided a correct answer.

Challenge: We had to try many prompts to get higher-difficulty questions because LLMs tended to generate trivial ones like "what is the size of the dataset".Insight: We broke this into two steps because LLMs tended to hallucinate answers:.

The complete prompting strategy and implementation is available in generate_qa.py.

In a recent development, finally we want to generate clean code execution traces since even the original notebooks after processing are often open ended and verbose with lots of irrelevant parts. However, we want our Jupyter Agent to get to the result efficiently. To generate cleaner notebook traces for training we generated traces synthetically based on the original notebooks.We have prompted Qwen-3-Coder-480B model to generate a jupyter notebook code to answer the question from the previously generated synthetic QA pair. Traces captured step-by-step code execution, including intermediate outputs, which are crucial for agent training.

We used E2B for our agent to solve the synthetic QA pairs, which required fetching Kaggle datasets so the code could actually run via E2B.

Challenge 1: Many datasets were unavailable.Trick: Since LLMs are strong at code and have a decent world model, we prompted them to act as a code interpreter when the dataset was missing.

Recent findings suggest that challenge 2: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B model does not support thinking mode - how can we extract code commentary? By default it often outputs just a brief comment followed by several steps of code execution. However, we'd like some reasoning or comments between every cell. Trick: When switching from Qwen3-32B to Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B we noticed that often output message content was empty. This turns out to be a previously known quirk of Qwen3-Coder models in which when using tool calling the model would not return an empty assistant response. We enforce some text commentary through tooling by passing 'comment' as a required field in the code execution tool call. This way when non-reasoning model is used for code cell generation it will by default output some description of its actions from 1st POV, emulating the thinking traces structure.

Note: the generated final answer in the notebook may vary from the answer specified in the QA pair. This is caused by the fact that the agent model could use data preprocessing methods and steps different from the original Kaggle notebook and the synthetic question would not usually specify them. This discrepancy is normal and lays the foundation for a new exciting research direction of how language models tend to treat data analysis and whether they do it differently from humans. For full transparency we keep both LLM-generated final answer and original answer from the real Kaggle notebook as a signal of model's performance. We encourage the community to try different dataset mixes to see how they can push performance even further.

We truncated overly long outputs and filtered out trivial traces to prevent content length issues and keep only high-quality traces.We kept non-trivial, multi-turn traces aligned with DABStep-style tasks.The resulting Jupyter Agent Dataset became the foundation for SFT on Qwen3-4B models with 51k synthetic notebooks and almost 0.2B tokens.

With this dataset in hand, the natural next step is to see whether it actually helps our model become a stronger data science agent. Let’s move on to the training pipeline and evaluate the impact!

In a recent development, with the curated dataset ready, we turned to the key question: does this data actually help the model get better at solving data analysis tasks? To find out, we set up a simple fine-tuning pipeline and ran experiments to measure the impact of training on our synthetic notebooks.

Some training steps turned out to be particularly interesting and gave us useful insights:.

Our complete training implementation, including hyperparameter configurations and template adaptations, is available in our finetuning directory in our repo.

It has been revealed that first, we generated our final dataset using Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B which contains high quality code and short reasoning-like traces. Afterwards, we started our training and we have experimented with various configurations like PEFT/adapters vs. full-parameter tuning, learning rate, number of epochs, adding noise and others. We found out, that full-parameter fine-tuning allows the model to learn and replicate the Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B behavior response quality better with shorter supporting commentary fitting more to the data analysis task without unnecessary long reasoning.

We have done a small ablation study on the impact of no. training epochs:.

Sources indicate that we observe that it is beneficial to have a bit more epochs than usual for SFT with lower learning rate and higher neftune noise (7). Finally, we compare our trained models with implemented scaffolding to define the pure impact of our training dataset. In summary, we can see up to 36%/22% boost on DABStep easy score compared with base/scaffolded model:.

We can also see, that the hard score can increase too even though our dataset is focused on easier questions:.

From figures above one can notice a noticeable impact of both new scaffolding and tuning on our synthetic notebooks. This makes Qwen-4B (with our pipeline + scaffolding) a state-of-the-art small-model agent on DABStep.

In practice, the model can now solve a wide range of realistic Kaggle-style data analysis tasks with consistent execution.It’s not yet strong enough for the hardest queries, but we’ve shown that even small models can become powerful agents when paired with the right data and scaffolding.

These results demonstrate that even small models can become powerful data science agents with the right training approach. Ready to try it yourself? We've made everything openly available so you can experiment with our fine-tuned models and dataset.

We openly release best-performing checkpoints of tuned Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 together with the training dataset, which you can try out and experiment with:.

It has been revealed that the best accounts receivable software for your tech giant is the layer that closes the stage where your cash leaks. If buyers settle from an emailed link and outreach starts late, a reminders tool covers most of it. If customers prefer to pay online by card or ACH, add a payments network with a customer portal. If clients require invoice uploads to Coupa or Ariba and clear multiple invoices with one blank-memo wire, you need an AR automation layer on top of the ERP. Every platform listed here serves B2B businesses invoicing other companies, excluding consumer payment apps and collection agencies.

Our source material is each vendor's public product, integration, security and pricing pages, plus G2 reviews, as they stood in November 2026.

About three in five US suppliers let business clients pay within 30 days, per Atradius's 2026 US payment practices survey (September 2026). Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:.

What invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

The ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

Layer: AI-native AR automation, for Series A to Fortune 500 finance teams.

Published pricing: Pricing scales with business volume and isn't a percentage of collections.

Leak it closes: Unapplied cash first, then stalled replies and portal rejections.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Cash application, where CashMatch AI handles wires that pay several invoices at once and payments that arrive without remittance.

Layer: Payments network and AR suite.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Invoice delivery into buyer portals, through 260+ AP portal integrations run from one interface.

Layer: AR automation layer with AI agents, on the ERP.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Customer replies that carry a promise-to-pay date or a dispute.

Layer: Payments network with customer portal.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Payment acceptance, through a customer portal for paying and disputing invoices online.

Layer: Reminders tool with AI reply drafts, on Xero and QuickBooks.

Leak it closes: Replies that sit unanswered at small and midsize companies.

Published pricing: US $259, $779 or $1,169 a month by annual revenue band; annual billing saves 10%.

Leak it closes: Follow-up timing, with reminders sent from your own email address on a schedule that escalates.

It has been revealed that on Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

Industry observers note that portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

Recent findings suggest that if your team still keys card numbers or chases ACH details, start with the payments layer. A payments network with a customer portal gives buyers stored methods and autopay. Unless the vendor indicates otherwise, it won't read replies or file into buyer portals, so proposal an AR layer for those stages.

Whether it's a medical AI trained on clinical data, a coding assistant optimized for a particular programming language, or a multilingual model fine-tuned for specific cultural contexts, the Hugging Face Hub has become the beating heart of open-source AI innovation.

In a recent development, but here's the challenge: finding an amazing model is just the beginning. What happens when you discover a model that's 90% perfect for your use case, but you need that extra 10% of customization? Traditional fine-tuning infrastructure is complex, expensive, and often requires significant DevOps expertise to set up and maintain.

Sources indicate that this is exactly the gap that Together AI and Hugging Face are bridging today. We're announcing a powerful new capability that makes the entire Hugging Face Hub available for fine-tuning using Together AI's infrastructure. Now, any compatible LLM on the Hub, whether it's from Meta or an individual contributor, can be fine-tuned with the same ease and reliability you expect from Together's platform.🚀.

Here's all it takes to start fine-tuning a HF model on the Together AI platform:.

Industry observers note that that's it! Your model will be trained on Together's infrastructure and can be deployed for inference, downloaded or even uploaded back to the Hub! For private repositories, simply add your HF token with hf_api_token="hf_xxxxxxxxxxxx".

As seen in the example above, when you fine-tune a Hugging Face model on Together AI, you actually specify two models:.

Think of the base model as a "training template." It tells our system how to optimally allocate GPU resources, configure memory usage, set up the training pipeline, and prepare the model for inference. Your custom model should have a similar architecture, approximate size, and sequence length to the base model for optimal results.

As seen in the example above, if you want to fine-tune HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct (which uses Llama architecture), you'd use togethercomputer/llama-2-7b-chat as your base model template, because they share the same underlying architecture.

The integration works bidirectionally. Together AI can pull any compatible public model from the Hugging Face Hub for training, and with the proper API tokens, it can download models private repositories as well. After training, your fine-tuned model can be automatically pushed back onto the Hub if you've specified hf_output_repo_name, making it available for sharing with your team or the broader community.

Recent findings suggest that in general, all CausalLM models under 100B params are intended to work. For a comprehensive walkthrough on how to choose base and custom models and much more, read our full guide!

Industry observers note that this integration solves a real problem many of us have faced: finding a great model on Hugging Face but not having the infrastructure to actually fine-tune it for your specific needs. Now you can go from discovering a promising model to having a customized version running in production with just a few API calls.

The substantial win here is removing friction. Instead of spending days setting up training infrastructure or being limited to whatever models are officially supported by various platforms, you can now experiment with any compatible model from the Hub. Found a specialized coding model that's close to what you need? Train it on your data!📈.

Industry observers note that for teams, this means faster iteration cycles. You can test multiple model approaches swiftly, build on community innovations, and even use your own fine-tuned models as starting points for further customization.

Beta owners and early adopters of this feature are already seeing results across diverse use cases.

Slingshot AI has integrated this capability directly into their model development pipeline. Rather than being limited to Together's model catalog, they can now run parts of the training pipeline on their own infrastructure, upload those models to the Hub, and then perform continued fine-tuning of those models using the Together AI fine-tuning platform. This has dramatically accelerated their development cycles and allowed them to easily experiment with a broad variety of model variants.

Parsed has demonstrated the power of this approach in their work showing how small, well-tuned open-source models can outperform much larger closed models. By fine-tuning models on carefully curated datasets, they've achieved superior performance while maintaining cost efficiency and full control over their models.

Common usage we're seeing from other customers include:.

According to recent reports, the most significant advantage teams report is speed to value. Instead of spending weeks setting up training infrastructure or months training models from scratch, they can identify promising starting points from the community and have specialized models running in production within days.

Cost efficiency is another major benefit. By starting with models that already have relevant capabilities, teams need fewer training epochs and can use smaller datasets to achieve their target performance, dramatically reducing compute costs.

Perhaps most importantly, this approach gives teams access to the collective intelligence of the open-source community. Every breakthrough, every specialized adaptation, every novel architecture becomes a potential starting point for their own work.

As expected with a large feature of this nature, we're actively improving the experience based on real usage, so your feedback directly shapes the platform!

#103641. Latest Update: The hidden human intelligence of design

Latest Update: The hidden human intelligence of design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.” Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility. We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities. DESIGN AND EMOTION Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value. Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user. A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision. Architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions. IMPACT VERSUS HOURS There’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log? I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done quickly and simply. The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining. It’s notable for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact. 6 DESIGN AREAS REQUIRING HUMAN SKILLS Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise: 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties. 2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom. 3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them. 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly. 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they stated understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear. 6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability. When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective. Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability.

When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s vital we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective.

Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

Tricks from OpenAI gpt-oss YOU 🫵 can use with transformers
